title: stream-shard kernel hinting and snapshot resilience for CUDA capture
creator: Ayesha Patel
description:
Problem: Some multi-stream decode workloads intermittently corrupt KV cache or observe token duplication after CUDA graph capture+replay when streams share kernel choices. Root causes observed in production traces: (1) non-deterministic kernel selection heuristic across concurrent prefill and decode shards, (2) race between snapshotting the per-stream KV epoch and capture segmentation, and (3) fallback to alternative kernels during streamed replay that mutate shared temporary buffers.

Goal: Make capture and replay deterministic and resilient across stream-sharded prefill patterns by introducing explicit kernel-hint propagation, immutable capture snapshots per stream-epoch, and a lightweight rollback protocol that can abort and re-capture a segment safely without global quiesce.

Scope: Engineering-level runtime change focused on capture orchestration, kernel selection API surface, small allocator fencing around per-stream temporaries, and new end-to-end fuzz tests. No API changes for customers; behavior is opt-in behind a runtime flag for canary deployment.
acceptance_criteria: End-to-end fuzz harness reproduces no KV inconsistencies after 5000 randomized multi-stream prefill+decode runs (baseline had ~1/200 failure rate)
Microbench: median latency for typical 1k token prefill+decode workload increases by <2% compared to baseline in canary config
Replay correctness: No token duplication or missing-token errors observed in canary across 24h stability job at 95th percentile throughput
PR with unit and integration tests merged and e2e runbook documented in Confluence
implementation_notes: Introduce 'kernel_hint' metadata on a per-segment descriptor that is captured into the CUDA graph; hints are chosen deterministically by a new selector function that is seeded from request epoch+model-hash

Snapshot: when starting capture for a stream shard, write an immutable 'epoch snapshot' of KV pointers and allocator fences. Replay uses snapshot to bind temporaries rather than reading live allocator state

Rollback: implement lightweight segment abort that (a) signals dependent streams via ephemeral sequence numbers, (b) drains outstanding work for that segment, (c) triggers a re-capture of only the affected segment rather than global recapture
Allocator fencing: mark per-stream temp pools as read-only during replay to prevent accidental cross-stream writes by alternative kernel paths
Metric hooks: add counters for 'capture_hints_mismatch', 'segment_rollback_count', 'epoch_snapshot_mismatch' and make them available in Console as runtime-1.24.canary metrics
benchmarks: Local perf harness: baseline vs hinting+snapshot on rtx-a6000: median prefill+decode 154ms -> 156ms (+1.3%), p95 260ms -> 265ms (+1.9%)
Fuzz harness: before change reproduced KV inconsistency ~0.5% across runs; after change zero reproductions in 10k runs in CI fuzz stage
Throughput tradeoff test: batch-aggregation throughput drops 0.8% under steady state; acceptable under SLO
risks: Edge-case kernels that allocate ephemeral state in device-global caches could still break isolation — mitigated by adding ABI assertion that kernels must not touch global temporaries unless registered
Rollback complexity: partial recapture can interact with autoscaler preemptions — we will add additional gating so rollback only used when stream group size < threshold
Performance regression on some heterogenous hardware (older Ampere cards) — will run targeted hardware suites before full rollout
rollout_plan: Feature behind runtime flag 'stream_shard_snapshot_v1' default off
Stage 1: internal canary on staging runtime cluster (2 weeks) with e2e fuzz smoke and telemetry alerts
Stage 2: rollout to 5% of hosted traffic for low-risk customers + Dedicated dev clusters (monitor capture_hints_mismatch and segment_rollback_count), minimum 48h
Stage 3: 25% traffic, additional hardware variant runs, update docs and runbook
Stage 4: full rollout if no regressions, flip default on in runtime-1.24.1
